# The Call of Character

Living a Life Worth Living

Mari Ruti

Columbia University Press

Should we feel inadequate when we fail to be healthy, balanced, and well-adjusted? Is it realistic or even desirable to strive for such an existential equilibrium? Condemning our current cultural obsession with cheerfulness and "positive thinking," Mari Ruti calls for a resurrection of character that honors our more eccentric frequencies and argues that sometimes a tormented and anxiety-ridden life can also be rewarding.
Ruti critiques the search for personal meaning and pragmatic attempts to normalize human beings' unruly and idiosyncratic natures. Exposing the tragic banality of a happy life commonly lived, she instead emphasizes the advantages of a lopsided life rich in passion and fortitude. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The Gulag Archipelago: An Experiment in Literary Investigation (Russian: Архипелаг ГУЛАГ, romanized: Arkhipelag GULAG) is a three-volume nonfiction series written between 1958 and 1968 by Russian writer Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn, a Soviet dissident. ... Finished in 1968, The Gulag Archipelago was microfilmed and smuggled out to Solzhenitsyn's main legal representative, Fritz Heeb of Zürich, to await publication; a later paper copy, also smuggled out, was signed by Heinrich Böll at the foot of each page to prove against possible accusations of a falsified work.

### About the author (2002)

Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn was born in Kislovodsk, Russia, in 1918. A twice-decorated captain in the Soviet Army, he was stripped of his rank, arrested, and convicted in 1945 for privately criticizing Stalin. Exiled from the USSR in 1974, Solzhenitsyn eventually settled in the United States before returning to his homeland twenty years later. Among his other acclaimed works are the novels One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich and The First Circle. His literary awards include the Nobel Prize for Literature and the Medal of Honor for Literature.

Paris holds a ceremony in honor of Alexander Solzhenitsyn, and freedom in Russia
Date: Fri Jan 31 02:38:36 2025 UTC

"For a free Russia..." Between past and present, on Thursday, January 30, the son of Alexander Solzhenitsyn (1918-2008) paid tribute not only to his father but also to all those who made it possible for <em>The Gulag Archipelago</em> to be published in Paris in December 1973. "It is well known to thoughtful people – or rather to people whose spiritual flair is not dead –that one of the most important rights of the peoples of the earth is the right to memory," said Ignat Solzhenitsyn, 52.
On the cobblestones of 11 Rue de la Montagne-Sainte-Geneviève, home of the legendary Franco-Russian bookshop Les Editeurs Réunis in the 5<sup>th</sup> arrondissement, he was the guest of honor at the ceremony to unveil the plaque honoring "the Russian writer, winner of the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1970, a great figure of resistance to totalitarianism."
Ignat<strong> </strong>Solzhenitsyn, now a conductor based in the US, and the other speakers at the ceremony recalled the role of the various key players who led to the publication in the West of <em>The Gulag Archipelago</em>, the book the Kremlin wanted to ban. From the anonymous and discreet French diplomat stationed in Moscow who had managed to exfiltrate the banned work out of Russia, to Nikita Struve, director at the time of YMCA-Press, the publishing house also known as Les Editeurs Réunis bookshop.
Russian embassy not invited

"This publication was an important moment in our lives, in our relationship with Russia, and also for our attachment to freedom," said Hervé Mariton, a former MP (Union for a Popular Movement) and minister in 2007, and one of the organizers, in 2018, of the Solzhenitsyn centenary in France. In the winter of 1973, as a Russian-speaking high-school student, he came to Rue de la Montagne-Sainte-Geneviève in search of one of the first translated copies of <em>The Gulag Archipelago</em>.
An immense fresco of the Soviet concentration camp universe, the work was written in secret from thousands of letters and testimonies received by Solzhenitsyn following the publication of his novel <em>One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich</em>. This veritable "literary investigation," as he put it, revealed to the world the scale of the Gulag system, that archipelago where millions of "zeks" (prisoners) died.
The Russian embassy in Paris was not invited to the ceremony unveiling the commemorative plaque. In the window of the bookshop Les Editeurs Réunis, another book now accompanies the various editions published, over five decades, of <em>The Gulag Archipelago </em>− <em>Patriot</em>, the posthumous book by Alexei Navalny, Vladimir Putin's most famous Kremlin opponent, who mysteriously died in prison on February 16, 2024.
